A design question—not a claim that learning outcomes have already been measured
How can an 8–12-year-old see that power, water, food and shelter depend on one another?
Every choice changes the same mission ledger; some effects arrive later.

The project addresses a design question: whether a short interactive mission can make linked resource trade-offs concrete for children ages 8–12. The deck presents this as an intended design goal only. No child user study or learning-outcome measurement is documented.
Science-inspired choices with an explicit boundary between NASA evidence and game rules
Each day introduces a new mission-planning situation.
Compare an immediate cost with a possible later benefit.
Mission Control returns a server-calculated change for every resource.
Short science signals link each theme to a NASA source.

text: MoonBase is a browser-based, four-planning-round educational game. The frontend displays backend-provided event choices and resource outcomes. It is an independent project; NASA source links inform themes and do not imply NASA endorsement or validation.
One loop, repeated across four days
Each in-game day is a planning round, not a real Earth day or lunar daylight cycle
Read the event and science signal.
Backend replays the full choice history.
Review daily, delayed, event and choice effects.
If any resource reaches 0, the run ends; after Day 4, Shelter readiness must be at least 6.

The backend is the single rules engine. For each submitted ordered history it recomputes from the canonical Day 1 values, validates choices, applies the deterministic rules, clamps each integer resource to 0–12, and returns the event or result plus a breakdown. A zero Power, Water, or Food ends the mission on that day. Success after Day 4 requires Power, Water, and Food above zero and Shelter readiness at least 6. There is no random event, score, rescue, extra day, database, or saved progress.
Four game meters · one shared budget
All quantities are integer game values on a 0–12 scale, not engineering units

Daily use:  Power −2 · Water −2
Food −2 · Shelter readiness −1

Array plan → Power on Days 2–4
Recycler service → Water on Days 3–4
Grow tray → Food on Day 4
Shelter prep → no readiness wear Days 2–4
Before + Daily + Scheduled + Event + Choice → clamp 0–12

Canonical initial values are Power 12, Water 12, Food 10, and Shelter readiness 8. Every resource is an integer from 0 to 12. Daily needs subtract 2 Power, 2 Water, and 2 Food; shelter readiness loses 1 except when Day 1 shelter preparation prevents wear on Days 2–4. Delayed effects: array cleaning adds Power +1 on Days 2–4; recycler service returns Water +1 on Days 3–4; grow tray adds Food +3 on Day 4. For every resource and day: After = clamp(Before + Daily + Scheduled + Event + Choice, 0, 12). These are game-only balance values, not NASA specifications.
Event names and choice effects below match the running game

Clean array: −1 Power now; +1 on Days 2–4.

Spare battery: +1 Power now.

Prepare shelter: −1 Power, +2 readiness; removes readiness wear Days 2–4.

Service recycler: −1 Power, +1 Water now; +1 Water on Days 3–4.

Backup pack: −3 Power, +5 Water now (capped at 12).

Start LED grow tray: −2 Power, −1 Water; +3 Food on Day 4.

Open meal crate: +3 Food now; no later harvest.

Solar-particle alert: −2 Shelter readiness.

Full setup: −1 Power, +4 readiness.

Low-power plan: no Power cost, +2 readiness; relies on earlier preparation.

The event text and selectable effects are taken from the actual rules service and live game. A Day is a planning round, not one Earth day or lunar daylight cycle. On Day 4 the implemented event is named 'A solar storm warning' and its narrative identifies a solar-particle alert. The app does not model atmospheric weather or an Earth-style lunar dust storm. All costs, bonuses, timing and thresholds are game-only values. NASA science caveats are on Slide 8. Sources: NASA NTRS lunar dust report https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20240003496 ; NASA ISS water recovery https://www.nasa.gov/missions/station/nasa-achieves-water-recovery-milestone-on-international-space-station/ ; NASA Advanced Plant Habitat https://science.nasa.gov/mission/advanced-plant-habitat/ ; NASA Orion shelter article https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/heliophysics/how-nasa-will-protect-astronauts-from-space-radiation-at-the-moon/.
NASA evidence inspires themes; game values stay fictional
Qualitative science cues are sourced; the simulation is not an engineering model
NASA documents lunar dust adhesion and array risks. The game's 'clean array' benefit is invented; NASA warns manual brushing can worsen damage.
The ISS demonstrated a 98% recovery goal. MoonBase's Water points do not use that percentage and are not a lunar system.
NASA's Advanced Plant Habitat uses LEDs and controlled water/nutrients. A one-turn game harvest compresses real growth time.
NASA ECLSS manages pressure, oxygen, air and water; MoonBase has no oxygen or pressure meter. NASA's Orion supplies shelter is a concept; readiness points are not a dose or shielding estimate.
The Moon has a thin exosphere; lunar 'weather' comes from space. Day 4 is a particle alert, not an atmospheric dust storm.

No real engineering units.

No lunar habitat design.

No radiation dose, shielding thickness, crop yield, or recovery efficiency calculation.
NASA sources support the science themes; they do not endorse or validate MoonBase.

Scientific claims and their sources: [1] NASA/TM-20240003496, Lunar Dust Considerations for Vertical Solar Arrays Vol. 1, published 1 Oct 2024, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20240003496. The report describes dust adhesion/abrasion and risks to exposed array surfaces; its PDF warns that manual brushing can damage arrays and is not recommended. The game's clean-array action is a fictional choice and should not be treated as a real cleaning recommendation. [2] NASA, NASA Achieves Water Recovery Milestone on International Space Station, 20 Jun 2023, https://www.nasa.gov/missions/station/nasa-achieves-water-recovery-milestone-on-international-space-station/. The 98% goal was demonstrated by ISS ECLSS; no game Water value represents 98% recovery. [3] NASA Science, Advanced Plant Habitat, https://science.nasa.gov/mission/advanced-plant-habitat/. The ISS facility uses LED lights and controlled delivery of water/nutrients; Day 4 harvest is compressed game time. [4] NASA, Environmental Control and Life Support Systems, https://www.nasa.gov/reference/environmental-control-and-life-support-systems-eclss/. ECLSS controls pressure, oxygen, ventilation, waste and water; MoonBase tracks no oxygen or pressure. [5] NASA Science, How NASA Will Protect Astronauts From Space Radiation at the Moon, 7 Aug 2019, https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/heliophysics/how-nasa-will-protect-astronauts-from-space-radiation-at-the-moon/. NASA describes a representative Orion temporary shelter using onboard supplies during an SEP event; this is not a lunar base design. Game Shelter readiness 0–12 is abstract, not dose or shielding. [6] NASA Science, Weather on the Moon, https://science.nasa.gov/moon/weather-on-the-moon/. NASA explains the Moon's exosphere is too thin for Earth-like weather; lunar weather comes from space. The game uses a solar-particle alert and does not model an atmospheric dust storm. No NASA endorsement or validation is claimed.
A real Day 2 choice in the running game
The selected path trades power now for water now and later
Spend 1 Power, gain 1 Water now, then use 1 less Water on Days 3 and 4.
Backup pack: spend 3 Power for 5 Water now (capped at 12), with no later reduction in Water use.

text: Screenshot captured from the actual running game on 27 Oct 2026. The Day 2 state followed Day 1's Connect the spare battery choice: Power 11, Water 10, Food 8, Shelter readiness 7. The service choice spends 1 Power and gains 1 Water immediately, then reduces Water use by one game unit on Days 3 and 4. Alternative backup pack costs 3 Power and adds 5 Water up to the 12 maximum, with no later water-use reduction. The in-game science signal references NASA's ISS water recovery milestone: https://www.nasa.gov/missions/station/nasa-achieves-water-recovery-milestone-on-international-space-station/. Its 98% figure is explicitly not applied to game values.
Mission Control shows the cost and payoff
The game returns a breakdown instead of hiding the resource arithmetic
Carry-over: Water use is 1 lower on Days 3–4. All values remain game units.

The exact returned result was Power 8/12 (Before 11; daily −2; choice −1), Water 9/12 (Before 10; daily −2; choice +1), Food 6/12 (Before 8; daily −2), Shelter readiness 6/12 (Before 7; daily −1). The server also scheduled Water use one game unit lower on Days 3 and 4. This example is from the actual battery → recycler route, not the separate documented worked route that cleans the array.

text: Actual final result captured in local browser after the sequence Connect the spare battery → Service the recycler → Start the LED grow tray → Power the full shelter setup. The live game declared mission complete and returned (Power 1, Water 6, Food 5, Shelter readiness 6), all game-value units. This path differs from the canonical worked path in docs/GAME_RULES.md (which begins with clean_solar_array and ends at (2,6,5,6)); both satisfy the implemented success criteria. No real lunar-survival or engineering performance is implied.
What players are invited to practice
Intended learning objectives · no child study or outcome measurement is documented
Notice that energy, water, food and shelter readiness share one mission budget.
Weigh an immediate cost against a scheduled benefit on a future round.
Use the feedback breakdown to explain how a choice changed the state.
Recognize NASA science themes while questioning simplified game values.
These are goals for play, not measured learning gains.

README and source confirm a plain static HTML/CSS/vanilla JavaScript frontend and a Java 17 Spring Boot 4.1.2 backend. The backend replays the complete ordered history and owns resource calculations and outcomes. No database/accounts/saved mission progress are used. docs/JUDGES_BRIEFING.md records backend 9 tests passed, frontend 3 tests passed, and a browser walkthrough/responsive checks. These tests were not rerun for this deck. During this presentation task the local health route returned UP and a full successful route was completed in the local browser; that live verification used a different successful route than the docs' clean-array path. No child study, NASA endorsement/validation, public deployment URL, production-origin CORS test or performance measurement is documented.
